analysisMarkdown:
## Where the price sits

Spot gold is $3,548.88, up 1.04% over the past 24 hours but still within touching distance of a fresh 52-week low of $3,533 set today. The recovery intraday does little to change the broader picture: price is **35.4% below the 52-week high of $5,496** reached on 2026-01-29. This is emphatically not record territory — it is the lower end of the past year's range.

The trend structure is negative on every timeframe that matters:

- **20-day return:** -8.9%
- **90-day return:** -22.7%
- **One-year return:** -12.6%
- **Spot vs 50-day average ($4,024):** -11.8%
- **Spot vs 200-day average ($4,239):** -16.3%

With both key moving averages well above spot and the 50-day sitting 5.1% below the 200-day, the market is in a clear downtrend. The 20-day closing range runs from $3,533 to $4,121, and annualised 20-day volatility is 32% — elevated, which means daily swings in either direction can be large.

## The macro backdrop

The macro setting is working against gold on two of its most important levers:

- **The dollar.** The Federal Reserve's trade-weighted **broad dollar index is 122.65**, up 0.65 over 30 days and 3.75 over 90 days, and higher than 100% of readings in the past year. A dollar near a one-year high makes gold more expensive for buyers outside the United States and is a persistent headwind.
- **Real yields.** The **10-year real yield is 2.88%**, up 0.11 pp over 30 days and 0.48 pp over 90 days, higher than 96% of the past year's readings. Because gold pays no income, rising real yields raise the opportunity cost of holding it.

Nominal 10-year Treasury yields are 5.04%, down 0.08 pp over 30 days but up 0.30 pp over 90 days, while the 10-year inflation breakeven has eased to 2.16%. In short, the real-yield increase is being driven more by firmer rates than by falling inflation expectations — a combination that typically pressures gold.

## Short-term outlook (1–4 weeks)

The short-term scorecard reads **-2, a baseline SELL at medium confidence**. The components:

- 20-day return of -8.9% → strongly adverse
- Spot 11.8% below the 50-day average → adverse
- The same -11.8% stretch counts as mildly **supportive** on a contrarian basis, since a price that has already fallen far from its average can snap back
- The 30-day moves in real yields and the dollar are both small enough to read as neutral

The net message is that downside momentum dominates, with only the degree of the recent decline offering any counterweight. This is a description of conditions, not advice. **This view would change on a daily close above $4,121.**

## Long-term outlook (3–12 months)

The long-term scorecard is unambiguous at **-6, a baseline SELL at high confidence**. All six measured factors point the same way:

- Price 16.3% below the 200-day average
- 50-day average 5.1% below the 200-day average
- 90-day return of -22.7%
- Spot 35.4% below the 52-week high
- Real yield up 0.48 pp over 90 days
- Broad dollar up 3.15% over 90 days

When trend, distance-from-high, yields and the dollar all line up negatively, the setup over the next 3–12 months looks more challenging than supportive. **This view would change on a daily close above $4,673.**

## Adjustments

Both horizons default to **0 steps**. An adjustment requires a specific, dated event within the last 10 days (short) or 45 days (long) that points in gold's favour. The confirmed developments I could document — the 2.5% drop on 2026-11-20, a dollar at a one-year high, and real yields near a one-year high — all point the same direction as the scorecard. There is no dated bullish catalyst to justify nudging either call toward HOLD, so the standing SELL calls remain in place.

## Risks to the view

Risks run in both directions. **For the short-term SELL:** volatility is high at 32% annualised, and price is already stretched well below its 50-day average, so a sharp countertrend bounce is possible; a daily close above $4,121 would invalidate the call. **For the long-term SELL:** the dominant drivers are the dollar and real yields. A clear turn lower in either — for example, a dovish shift in Fed policy or a decisive drop in yields — could change the picture, and a daily close above $4,673 would break the long-term view. Conversely, the main downside risk is continuation: with the dollar and real yields both near one-year highs and momentum negative, further weakness cannot be ruled out. None of this is a recommendation about any individual's holdings — it is a reading of the measured conditions.
